sections.h2: How does selling a house in Maine work at the county and town level?
sections.html:
Maine has sixteen counties, but most of the day to day work on a house sale happens at the town or city level and at the county registry of deeds. Counties here do limited work. The Census Bureau, as quoted on Wikipedia's county list, says counties in Maine are responsible for only limited functions, such as some law enforcement, short-term jails and roads in areas with no local government.

That split matters when you list a property. Your tax bill comes from the municipality, the deed is recorded with the county, and an estate is handled by the county probate court. Three different offices can touch one sale. Our Maine guides by city and county collect the local details we have so far.

Here is who handles what.

  • The town or city assessor sets the assessed value and sends the property tax bill.
  • The county registry of deeds records the deed and collects the transfer tax.
  • The county probate court appoints a personal representative when an owner has died.

Hours, fees and filing rules differ from one office to the next, so call the office before you drive over or mail anything.

sections.h2: What do Maine sellers need to know about property taxes before closing?
sections.html:
Each municipality collects its own property tax, so your bill depends on your town. Under 36 M.R.S. section 505, a municipality votes on the dates taxes come due, the date interest starts and the interest rate. That vote also fixes the date a bill becomes delinquent. Two neighbors in different towns can face different deadlines on houses of the same value.

If you are behind, the unpaid amount normally has to be settled at closing or dealt with before it. Call the tax collector in your town for a payoff figure and ask what interest has built up. Our Maine property tax guide covers appeals, exemptions and what happens when tax stays unpaid.

Maine has a homestead exemption for a permanent resident who has owned a Maine homestead for the preceding twelve months. The statute at 36 M.R.S. section 683 starts with an exemption of $10,000 of just value and adds a local ratio adjustment. The break belongs to the person living in the house, so the next owner applies on their own. Details are on our homestead exemption page, and your town assessor can tell you whether you currently hold it.

sections.h2: Is foreclosure in Maine judicial or non-judicial, and how long does it take?
sections.html:
Maine foreclosure goes through the courts. Under 14 M.R.S. section 6321, a first-priority mortgagee starts with a civil action in the Superior Court or District Court in the division where the property sits. A judge then decides whether the borrower is in breach and how much is owed.

Several waiting periods apply, and they stack up. The steps below come from the statutes we read.

  • Before the lender can accelerate or enforce a mortgage on an owner-occupied home for a missed payment, it must wait at least 35 days after giving a written notice of the right to cure (14 M.R.S. section 6111).
  • If the court finds a breach, it enters a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The redemption period for mortgages after October 1, 1975 is 90 days from the date of judgment, provided no appeal is taken (section 6322).
  • After redemption ends, notice of a public sale runs once a week for three weeks, and the sale is held 30 to 45 days after the first publication (section 6323).

Until the sale happens, an owner can still sell the house and pay the lender from proceeds, which can protect credit and any equity. Talk with a Maine attorney or housing counselor about your exact dates. A cash buyer can often close faster than a typical listing, but nothing here is a promise about timing in your case.

sections.h2: What happens when you inherit a house in Maine?
sections.html:
An inherited house usually goes through the county probate court first. A personal representative is appointed, and that person has the power over estate title that an absolute owner would have, held for creditors and others with an interest. 18-C M.R.S. section 3-711 allows a sale without a court order in most cases.

The main limit is notice. The representative may not sell or transfer estate real property without giving at least 10 days of notice to anyone succeeding to an interest in it, unless the will authorizes a sale without that notice. Check the will early, because that one clause changes the schedule.

Heirs who disagree about who should serve or whether to sell can stall the whole thing. Our Maine probate guide walks through the steps, and our Maine estate tax page explains when an estate has to file even if no tax is owed. Ask the register of probate in the county where the owner lived for current forms and fees.

sections.h2: How much is the Maine transfer tax and who pays it?
sections.html:
Maine charges $2.20 for each $500, or fractional part of $500, of the value of the property transferred. Value above $1,000,000 carries an extra $3.80 per $500 on the portion over that line (36 M.R.S. section 4641-A). The statute puts half of the tax on the seller and half on the buyer.

For a quick example, a $300,000 sale is 600 units of $500, so the tax is $1,320 and each side owes $660. When you compare offers, ask in writing whether the buyer is paying your half. Our transfer tax guide has more examples, and our deed recording page explains where the deed is filed.

sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Maine and who do you call?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded at the registry of deeds in the county where the land lies. The registry is a county office, so it is not the same place as the town office that sends your tax bill.

Use this short list when you start.

  • Call your town assessor for the assessed value and exemption status.
  • Call the tax collector for the current balance and any interest.
  • Call the county registry of deeds about recording hours and fees.
  • Call the register of probate if the owner has died.

Our city and county guides and the county sections below link to the pages we have built for the places we cover. Fees and hours change, so confirm with the office.

sections.h2: What about tenants, radon and other issues that can come up in a Maine sale?
sections.html:
If tenants live in the house, the lease and Maine landlord rules shape what a buyer can do. Our landlord and tenant page and eviction page cover the basics. Get legal advice before you try to end a tenancy to sell.

Radon is a Maine specific item. The Maine CDC says that if a home is for sale, an independent registered radon tester must perform the test. Plan for that early, since a result can come up during a buyer's inspection.

Taxes on your gain are a separate question. Maine does not publish its own capital gains rate for home sales, and our capital gains page explains how the gain flows to your income tax return. A tax professional can run your numbers.

sections.h2: What does a cash as-is sale mean in Maine?
sections.html:
A cash sale as-is means the buyer pays without a mortgage and takes the house in its current condition. You skip repair lists, showings and many lender delays. You still have a purchase contract, a deed, transfer tax and a closing where the deed is recorded.

Before you accept any offer, find out who pays the transfer tax half, whether back taxes come out of your proceeds and who handles the title work. Compare the net figure after all of that, not only the headline number. Ask a Maine attorney or title professional to review the paperwork, as the rules above have details this page cannot settle for your property.

If you would like to talk it through, call us or send the form on this page. We buy houses across Maine, including the places listed below.

faqs.q: How many counties does Maine have?
faqs.a: Sixteen. The most populous is Cumberland County, which includes Portland and South Portland, and Androscoggin County holds Lewiston and Auburn. Bangor is in Penobscot County.

faqs.q: Is Maine foreclosure handled by a court?
faqs.a: Yes. The lender files a civil action in Superior Court or District Court. For owner-occupied homes a written right to cure notice must come first, and the borrower must be given at least 35 days from that notice.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period after a foreclosure judgment?
faqs.a: For mortgages after October 1, 1975 it is 90 days from the date of judgment, if no appeal is taken. Ask an attorney how your specific dates run.

faqs.q: Who pays the Maine transfer tax?
faqs.a: The tax is split in half between the seller and the buyer. The rate is $2.20 for each $500 of value, with an extra $3.80 per $500 on value over $1,000,000.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell an inherited house without court approval?
faqs.a: Often yes, since a personal representative has broad power over estate title. At least 10 days of notice must go to people who succeed to an interest, unless the will waives it.

faqs.q: Do I need a radon test to sell a Maine home?
faqs.a: The Maine CDC says an independent registered radon tester must perform the test when a home is for sale. Ask your agent or attorney how it applies to your sale.

faqs.q: Who sends my property tax bill?
faqs.a: Your town or city. Each municipality votes its own due dates and interest rules, so call the local tax collector for your balance.
